content: Allergic rhinitis is a highly prevalent chronic condition, affecting between 10% and 40% of children globally. Over the past two decades, there has been a marked increase in its prevalence among children, which has been accompanied by a corresponding rise in associated comorbidities, such as asthma. The objective of this study was to assess the therapeutic efficacy and safety profiles of topical nasal steroids in the management of intermittent and persistent allergic rhinitis in children. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Ear, Nose and Throat Disorders Group Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others, up to September 5, 2005. Additional searches were performed in databases such as CINAHL, mRCT, NRR, LILACS, MedCarib, KOREAMED, IndMed, Samed, Panteleimon, Zetoc, ISI Proceedings, and pharmaceutical company trial registries, including those of GlaxoSmithKline, AstraZeneca, Schering Plough, and Aventis. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials that compared different topical nasal steroid preparations or compared these steroids to placebo in the treatment of allergic rhinitis in children. Two independent reviewers evaluated the quality of the trials and extracted data. However, the limited and inconsistent quality of the available data prevented the pooling of results, and only a descriptive summary of the findings was possible. Three trials, involving a total of 79 participants, were included in the analysis. These trials compared the use of topical nasal steroids with placebo for the treatment of perennial allergic rhinitis. While some data relevant to the primary outcomes were provided, the quality of the data was poor. Two of the trials had flawed data analyses, and the third trial's data were incomprehensible. None of the trials provided information relevant to the secondary outcomes. Importantly, no adverse events were reported in any of the interventions. The authors concluded that the evidence from the three included trials was weak and unreliable regarding the effectiveness of Beconase® and flunisolide administered intranasally for the treatment of intermittent and persistent allergic rhinitis in children. The reduction in symptom severity, as assessed by the trial investigators, could not be confirmed based on the available data. Until more robust evidence becomes available, decisions regarding the use of these medications should be guided by the clinical judgment of the physician and tailored to the individual circumstances and preferences of the patient.
